subtype: Why people make and share fakes [Observer]
passage:
The tram in Oslo was packed and steamy after the storm. Lars held his phone up to Lindiwe: a shark swimming down a flooded street, right past a bus stop.
"Look at this! Near the harbour!"
Lindiwe tilted her head. "That shark has been in every storm since I was eight. Durban, Houston, now Oslo."
"Why would anyone fake that?"
"Loads of reasons. Some pages make money when you click. Some people want attention. Some fakes are made to make people angry at a politician or scared of a group. Some are just cruel."
"But my aunt shared it."
"Your aunt isn't lying. She shares it because it feels true. The storm was real, so the shark feels possible."
Lars looked at the photo again, calmer now. "So I shouldn't just ask if it's real. I should ask who gets something out of it."
"Exactly. Then you don't need to panic. You just wait."

qa.q: What did the photo on Lars's phone show?
qa.a: It showed a shark swimming down a flooded street, right past a bus stop.

qa.q: How did Lars's feeling change after Lindiwe explained?
qa.a: Lars moved from excitement to calm doubt; he looked at the photo again, calmer, and started thinking about who gains from it.

qa.q: Which question does Lars decide to ask about viral photos from now on?
qa.a: Lars decides to ask who gets something out of a photo, not only whether it is real, so he can doubt calmly instead of panicking.

qa.q: How does Lindiwe see Lars's aunt differently from the person who made the fake?
qa.a: Lindiwe sees the aunt as honest but fooled, sharing because it feels true, while the maker may want money, attention, anger or cruelty.

grounding: On a tram, Lindiwe explains to Lars that fakes are made for clicks, attention, politics or cruelty and shared by people who feel they are true.

subtype: Why people make and share fakes [Observer]
passage:
In the Class 9 computer lab, Simran ma'am pulled up two images on the projector. One was the fake notice that had gone round the week before, saying the school would close for a heatwave. The other was a cruel edited photo of a boy from another school, his face stretched into a pig's snout.
"Both of these were made by someone," she said. "Why?"
Bidisha raised her hand. "For fun?"
"Sometimes. Let's list them." On the board she wrote: money, clicks, politics, cruelty.
"The heatwave notice got a page thousands of new followers. That's clicks. The photo of the boy? Cruelty."
"But Didi forwarded the heatwave one," Bidisha said quietly. "She's not a liar."
"No. Most people who share fakes believe the feeling in them. It was hot. A holiday felt possible."
Bidisha wrote that down. It felt less like being tricked, more like seeing the machine.

qa.q: What four reasons did Simran ma'am write on the board?
qa.a: She wrote money, clicks, politics and cruelty.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel after hearing why people share fakes?
qa.a: Bidisha felt less foolish and calmer, as if she was seeing how the machine works instead of just being tricked.

qa.q: What makes Simran ma'am's lesson work well?
qa.a: She uses real examples the class has seen, lets students suggest reasons, and separates the makers' motives from the sharers who believe the feeling.

qa.q: How might Bidisha's Didi feel if she heard this lesson?
qa.a: Didi might feel relieved not to be called a liar, and more ready to pause next time because she understands why the notice felt true.

grounding: Simran ma'am explains that fakes are made for money, clicks, politics or cruelty and shared by people who believe the feeling, helping a student doubt calmly.

subtype: Why people make and share fakes [Observer]
passage:
Hi Anand bhaiya,
You asked why I've gone quiet in the family group. It's about Mama.
Every morning he forwards things: a "miracle cure" video, a photo of a flooded airport, a story about a politician that turned out to be from another country. Yesterday I checked three of them. All fake.
In civics, Pillai sir explained that fakes get made for different reasons: some people earn money from clicks, some want votes, some just enjoy upsetting others. Then he said the people who forward them usually aren't liars. They forward because the message feels true to them, even when the details are wrong.
That helped. Mama isn't trying to fool us. The flood photo scared him because Mami was travelling that day.
So I'm not going to fight him in the group. I'll sit with him on Sunday and show him how I checked.
Alka

qa.q: What reasons did Pillai sir give for why fakes get made?
qa.a: Some people earn money from clicks, some want votes, and some just enjoy upsetting others.

qa.q: How does Alka feel about Mama's forwards after the civics class?
qa.a: Alka feels calmer and more understanding, no longer angry, seeing that Mama forwards things because they feel true, not to fool anyone.

qa.q: What is Alka's plan, and why might it work better than arguing?
qa.a: Sitting with Mama on Sunday to show how the checking works; it avoids shaming him in the group and passes on a habit instead.

qa.q: Why might Mama have forwarded the flood photo?
qa.a: The photo scared Mama because Mami was travelling that day, so it felt true and urgent even though it was fake.

grounding: Shows a teenager watching a relative forward fakes and using a teacher's explanation of motives to doubt calmly instead of fighting.

subtype: Why people make and share fakes [Observer]
passage:
Okay, this is Pankaj, and for the school podcast I want to talk about the fake notice.
In March a notice went round saying our school was closed because of a gas leak. It had the logo, the principal's signature, everything. Half the class stayed home. I watched my neighbour Ritwik forward it to eleven groups. He wasn't lying on purpose. He genuinely looked scared for his little sister.
Later our friend Gautam found out who made it: a boy from another school who runs a meme page. He did it for followers. His page grew by thousands that day.
Gautam put it simply. Some people make fakes for money, some for clicks, some for power, some just to be cruel. And the people who share them usually believe them.
That changed something for me. Now when I see a shocking notice, I don't panic, and I don't blame the forwarder. I ask: who gains from this? Then I check the school's own page.

qa.q: Why did the fake notice say the school was closed?
qa.a: Because of a gas leak.

qa.q: How does Pankaj feel now when a shocking notice appears?
qa.a: Pankaj feels calm rather than panicked, asking who gains before checking the school's own page, and no longer blames the forwarder.

qa.q: What two-step check does Pankaj now use?
qa.a: Asking who gains from the message, then checking the school's own page before reacting or forwarding.

qa.q: Why did Ritwik forward the notice to eleven groups?
qa.a: Ritwik looked genuinely scared for his little sister, so the notice felt true to him even though it was fake.

grounding: Shows a teenager watching a neighbour share a fake notice and learning from a friend why fakes are made and why sincere people spread them.

subtype: Why people make and share fakes [Observer]
passage:
Everyone calls me Chinmay the backbencher, and from the back I saw Joseph's face when the screenshot came up. It showed a chat, supposedly from our maths teacher, mocking the weak students by name. Joseph's name was on it. He went red and forwarded it to the class group with "see what she really thinks of us".
By second period everyone had it. Mrs Thomas, our class teacher, walked in, put her phone on the desk and said, "Let's talk about this."
She showed us that the chat bubbles used the wrong font and the time said 25:10. Then she asked why someone would make it. Hands went up. "For fun." "For likes." "To get her in trouble." She nodded. "And why did people share it?"
Nobody answered. I looked at Joseph. He was staring at his desk. I'm not sure what he felt. I felt a bit sick, because I'd believed it too, and it was easier to believe about a teacher I didn't like.

qa.q: What time did the fake chat show?
qa.a: The time said 25:10.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel after the class discussion, and why?
qa.a: Chinmay felt a bit sick and ashamed, having believed the fake too, and noticing it was easier to believe about a teacher Chinmay didn't like.

qa.q: How did Mrs Thomas help the class doubt the screenshot calmly?
qa.a: She pointed out the wrong font and the impossible time, then asked why someone would make it and why people shared it, so motive became part of the check.

qa.q: Why might Joseph have forwarded the screenshot so quickly?
qa.a: Joseph's own name was on it, so it hurt and felt true to him, and he shared it before checking.

grounding: Shows a classmate watching a fake chat spread and a teacher explaining why fakes are made and shared, which makes calm doubt easier.

subtype: Why people make and share fakes [Observer]
passage:
Monday: Rashmi watched her cousin forward a video of a shark swimming down a flooded city street. Rashmi noticed it had no date or place, but said nothing.
Wednesday: In media class, Ms Sonali played the same clip. "It's edited. Old footage, somewhere else. So why would anyone make it?" Hands went up. "Money, from views." "Just to trick people." "To make one side look bad." Ms Sonali nodded. "And why do your aunties share it?" Silence. "Because it feels true. They're scared of floods, so a scary video fits. They're not lying; they believe it."
Saturday: At a family lunch, Rashmi's Mama forwarded a clip about a "poisoned" festival sweet. Rashmi didn't roll her eyes this time. "Mama, who do you think made this? And what would they get from it?" He paused, then laughed. "Views, I suppose." He didn't forward it again.

qa.q: What reasons did students give for making fakes?
qa.a: Money from views, to trick people, and to make one side look bad.

qa.q: How did Rashmi seem to feel at the family lunch, compared with Monday?
qa.a: Rashmi seemed calmer and more confident, asking Mama questions instead of staying silent or rolling her eyes.

qa.q: Why does asking about motive help?
qa.a: Asking who made it and what they would gain lets people doubt calmly without feeling accused, as happened with Mama.

qa.q: Why might Rashmi's Mama have forwarded the clip in the first place?
qa.a: He probably felt it was true or worrying rather than wanting to lie, just as Ms Sonali said about the aunties.

grounding: Shows a teacher explaining that fakes are made for money, clicks, politics or cruelty and shared by people who believe them, and a teen using that to doubt calmly.
